title: Observability and Path Health

Overlapping Spans and the Critical Path
Keeping the Spans of One Trace Together
Measuring the Fix During a Canary
Design Exercise: Observability for Document Processing

html:
Have you ever completed a payment, watched the page continue loading, and wondered whether the transaction went through? You might check your email, refresh the page, or open your banking application to see whether a charge appeared. If the application still shows a pending order, you are left with the same question. Did the payment succeed, or should you try again?

A Baodium customer encountered this situation during checkout. After pressing Pay, the page continued loading without showing a confirmation. The customer refreshed and found the order listed as pending. A confirmation email arrived several minutes later, but by then the customer was worried that the refresh might have submitted another purchase.

Support found one order in Baodium’s database. Payment Service had recorded two authorization attempts, and the gateway logs showed that the original browser connection had closed before the response completed. Those records gave the support engineer pieces of the story, although they did not immediately explain how the attempts related to one another or which result the customer had received.

The infrastructure dashboards offered little help at first. CPU and memory usage were within their normal ranges. The payment provider had become slower, and database connection waits had increased, but there was no single record connecting the customer’s original submission to the payment attempts, the committed order, and the response returned by the gateway.

This is where observability becomes useful. The term originated in control theory, where it describes the ability to determine a system’s internal state from its observable outputs.1

For a production application, the question is practical. When a customer reports that something went wrong, can we reconstruct what the system actually did? And when a dashboard shows that an operation succeeded, what evidence supports that conclusion?

Baodium’s investigation began by separating three observations that the original monitoring had treated too loosely: the order committed in the database, the response sent by the gateway, and the result displayed in the customer’s browser.

What Each Observation Proves

Consider a checkout that authorizes payment and commits an order successfully. Order Service may have recorded everything correctly, yet the customer can still receive no confirmation if the connection closes before the response arrives.

The reverse also deserves attention. A server can finish sending a response without knowing whether the browser rendered it. A customer may close the tab, lose connectivity, or encounter a JavaScript error after the response arrives.

Baodium needed to observe the operation at three boundaries.

The first boundary was the authoritative database. The second was the gateway, where the HTTP request entered and its response ended. The third was the browser, where the customer submitted the operation and the interface attempted to display the result.

Figure Figure shows the distinction.

The Committed Business Result

At the database boundary, Order Service recorded state transitions in the same transaction as the business change.

When an order moved from pending to confirmed, its state record and the corresponding transition record committed together. If the transaction rolled back, neither change became durable.

That gave the engineers a reliable history of the business state. They could establish when an order was accepted, when payment was confirmed, and whether the operation eventually reached a terminal outcome.

A counter incremented separately in application code would provide a weaker guarantee. The database could commit successfully, followed by a process crash before the counter was incremented. Or the counter could be incremented before a transaction that later rolled back.

For authoritative business totals, the team used durable state records as the source and derived aggregate measurements from them.

This also made recovery easier. A reconciliation worker could inspect the recorded operation state after a process restart instead of depending on what the previous process had managed to report.

The Gateway Response

Baodium’s gateway recorded the outcome of each checkout HTTP request, including its route, status, duration, request identifier, and a protected reference to the business operation.

For a completed response, the gateway could establish that it processed the request and finished the server-side response handling.

It could not establish that the browser displayed the response.

The gateway also recorded connections closed before a response completed. Nginx, for example, uses the nonstandard status code 499 in access logs when a client closes the connection before the server finishes responding.

Baodium normalized those cases under a disconnected outcome.

That was important during the checkout investigation. Order Service could continue processing after the customer abandoned the original request. The gateway’s disconnection record described what happened to the HTTP exchange, while the operation record described what happened to the purchase.

The two records could disagree without either being incorrect.

What the Browser Displayed

The third observation came from the customer’s browser.

Baodium instrumented the checkout interface to report when the customer submitted an operation and when a result appeared in the interface.

A submission report identified the attempted operation. A display report identified the request and result associated with a rendered confirmation, rejection, or pending state.

The page used browser timing information and navigator.sendBeacon to submit reports without making the customer wait for the telemetry request to finish.

This was useful, but browser reporting was best-effort. A crashed tab, network failure, privacy setting, or blocked request could prevent a report from reaching Baodium.

An absent display report therefore did not prove that the customer saw nothing. It meant Baodium had no browser-side confirmation for that result.

Even a successfully received display report could establish only that the interface reached its instrumented display step. It could not prove that the customer noticed or understood what appeared on the screen.

The team treated those limits explicitly. A missing report was classified as unknown rather than counted as a successful display.

The gateway’s latency measurement also had a defined boundary. It started when the gateway began processing an eligible request and ended when the response completed or the request was otherwise terminated.

Browser connection setup, TLS negotiation, and page rendering required separate browser or network measurements.

These boundaries gave the engineers a more accurate way to answer the support ticket. They could establish which operation committed, what response the gateway attempted to return, and what the available browser reports showed, without treating one observation as proof of another.

Metrics, Logs, and Distributed Traces

Now suppose an engineer opens a dashboard showing that checkout latency increased over the last fifteen minutes. That is useful information, but the dashboard does not explain what one particular customer experienced.

The engineer might next search for the customer’s operation, examine the service events, and follow the request through Order Service and Payment Service.

This is why most observability systems use three complementary kinds of telemetry.

Metrics summarize measurements over many operations. They show request rate, failures, latency distributions, connection usage, and other quantities that change over time.

Logs record individual events with details needed for investigation. A payment attempt might record that it timed out, which provider account it used, and the operation reference associated with it.

Distributed traces connect operations performed during one execution. They show which services participated in a request, the order in which calls occurred, and how long each recorded step took.

Each kind of telemetry answers a different part of the investigation.

A metric can reveal that the slowest checkouts are taking six seconds instead of two. A trace can show that a particular checkout spent most of that time waiting for a database connection. The durable operation records and logs can then show whether the payment completed after the customer’s request stopped waiting.

There are limitations to all three.

Metrics need bounded labels because every new label combination consumes monitoring resources. Logs grow with the volume of events and must be protected from sensitive information. Traces may be sampled, and instrumentation gaps can hide part of a request.

The goal is to make the evidence useful together, including when one kind of telemetry is missing.

Collecting Telemetry Across Services

During the incident, the measurements on Baodium’s dashboards had passed through several systems before the on-call engineer opened them.

Application instrumentation created the measurements. Collection services received them, processing components applied the organization’s policies, and storage systems retained them for queries, dashboards, and alerts.

Baodium used OpenTelemetry for application instrumentation and collection.

The services exposed Prometheus-compatible metrics, which Prometheus scraped at a configured interval of fifteen seconds. OpenTelemetry Collector agents received traces and logs close to the application instances and forwarded them to a central collector tier.

Prometheus and Thanos retained metrics, Loki retained logs, and Tempo retained traces. Grafana supplied the dashboards, while Alertmanager routed notifications.

The particular products could be changed without changing the basic requirements. The engineers needed reliable collection, consistent attributes, reasonable cost, and a way to detect missing telemetry.

Pull and Push Collection

Prometheus uses a pull model for scraping targets. It requests metrics from an endpoint such as /metrics and records whether the scrape succeeded.

That gives the monitoring system a useful failure signal. When a target remains discoverable but cannot be scraped, its up metric becomes zero.

A push model behaves differently. An application or agent sends telemetry on its own schedule. If the producer stops running, data stops arriving.

The collector or backend therefore needs another way to distinguish a silent, healthy workload from one that has disappeared.

Baodium kept metrics on the Prometheus scrape path and used collectors for traces and logs.

The application SDKs batched telemetry and exported it asynchronously through bounded queues. That reduced the effect of slow telemetry backends on request handling, although generating telemetry still consumed some application CPU and memory.

The team tested exporter backpressure and queue overflow, since an overloaded collector must not introduce unbounded waiting into checkout.

Collector Processing and Correlation

Collector agents forwarded data to a central tier where shared processing rules were applied.

The collectors added deployment attributes, enforced permitted attribute sets, applied trace sampling, and buffered data within their configured limits.

Central processing reduced the number of policies application teams had to implement separately. It also created a shared dependency for telemetry delivery.

If the gateway collectors failed, many services could lose trace or log coverage at once.

The platform team therefore monitored the collectors themselves, including received spans, rejected data, exporter failures, queue utilization, and dropped records.

Correlation depended on consistent identifiers and attributes.

OpenTelemetry resource attributes such as service.name and service.version identified the emitting application. Deployment attributes recorded the environment and region.

Trace and span identifiers connected log records to traces, while exemplars could connect individual histogram observations to sampled traces.

With those links, an engineer could open a latency graph, find a representative slow request, and inspect the application events recorded during its execution.

Monitoring Services and Their Dependencies

Before diagnosing an individual checkout, the team first needed to know whether the required services were reachable.

Baodium had approximately forty services, each with multiple instances.

The platform team used several forms of monitoring because no single check could establish the health of every request path.

Health Checks and Service Discovery

Chapter 6 introduced Kubernetes startup, readiness, and liveness probes.

Those probes helped Kubernetes decide when an instance could receive traffic and when a restart might recover a local failure.

They did not establish that customers could complete a purchase through the entire checkout path.

Prometheus supplied another view.

For a discovered target, the up metric was one when the scrape succeeded and zero when it failed.

An alert on an instance whose up value remained zero could detect a process that was no longer exporting metrics.

There was a gap in this approach.

If an instance disappeared from service discovery, Prometheus might stop producing the corresponding up series entirely.

An alert evaluating only up == 0 would no longer see that instance.

Baodium compared discovered targets with expected instances and used absent checks for critical service-level metric coverage.

Kubernetes replica measurements provided another comparison, and the service catalog was checked against monitoring discovery on a schedule.

These checks identified missing monitoring coverage, including services that had never been discovered.

Request and Resource Measurements

An instance can pass its health checks while every customer request fails.

The services therefore reported request rate, errors, and duration, commonly called RED metrics.

For resources such as connection pools, the team also examined utilization, saturation, and errors, often called USE metrics.

Consider the database pool from Chapter 1.

The number of assigned connections described utilization. Pending acquisitions showed saturation. Acquisition timeouts and failed database operations described errors.

These measurements were more useful together than a single pool utilization percentage.

A pool could be near its limit while requests still completed promptly. A growing acquisition queue showed that demand was beginning to exceed available capacity.

External Probes

Internal monitoring has another blind spot.

Suppose Baodium’s DNS records become unreachable or its public TLS configuration breaks.

The services may continue running normally behind the gateway. Their CPU usage looks healthy, and their internal health checks succeed.

Customers still cannot reach the application.

Baodium used synthetic probes from three external locations to test its public endpoints.

Some verified DNS, TLS, and page responses. Others followed a controlled checkout using a test account and test payment method.

A separate probe retrieved the status of a known operation.

The probes ran at a bounded rate and used identifiable test data so that their requests could be excluded from business reporting without being excluded from infrastructure diagnostics.

Background Worker Progress

Reconciliation workers required another kind of check.

A worker could remain alive and continue responding to its health endpoint while making no progress on pending payments.

Baodium recorded the timestamp of the last successful recovery operation.

The monitoring system could then evaluate

time() - reconciliation_last_success_timestamp_seconds

An alert could fire when that interval exceeded the expected limit during periods when work was due.

The team also tracked backlog size and the age of the oldest unresolved operation.

A recent successful reconciliation did not establish that the worker was keeping up with incoming work.

Not every failed instance required paging an engineer. An isolated instance failure with sufficient healthy capacity could produce a ticket, while customer-facing failure or rapidly exhausted error budget required a faster response.

The next step in Baodium’s checkout investigation was to understand how many customers were affected and where their latency was increasing.

Request Metrics and Latency Distributions

The gateway exported a request counter and a duration histogram for checkout.

checkout_requests_total{route, region, version, outcome}

checkout_request_duration_seconds{
    route, region, version, outcome
}

The duration metric is a classic Prometheus histogram in the examples that follow.

Both instruments use the same bounded classification of eligible checkout requests.

The outcome label distinguishes five results:

confirmed.

Checkout returned a confirmed purchase.

rejected.

A definite business rejection was returned, such as a declined payment.

pending.

A durable operation was accepted and its status reference was returned.

failed.

The request failed without an acceptable customer result.

disconnected.

The customer connection ended before the response completed.

These distinctions mattered because ordinary HTTP error rate could overlook two important customer experiences.

Checkout might return pending responses quickly while fewer customers received final confirmations.

The median latency could improve even though the number of unresolved purchases was growing.

Alternatively, checkout could return correct confirmations while taking much longer than customers were willing to wait.

The dashboard therefore showed outcome rates, latency distributions, and the age of unresolved operations together.

Labels and Cardinality

The labels in a Prometheus metric allow engineers to select particular groups of requests.

A region label can identify a localized incident. A version label can compare a new deployment with its predecessor. The outcome label separates successful business responses from incomplete ones.

Every unique combination of metric name and label values creates another time series.

That property is called cardinality.

Suppose a service reports six regions, three versions, forty instances, and five outcomes.

Those dimensions produce

6×3×40×5=3,6006 \times 3 \times 40 \times 5 = 3{,}6006×3×40×5=3,600

label combinations for one route.

A classic histogram with eight finite bucket boundaries produces nine bucket series, including +Inf, plus a sum and a count.

That is eleven series per label combination, or

3,600×11=39,6003{,}600 \times 11 = 39{,}6003,600×11=39,600

time series for one latency metric.

Adding another high-cardinality label could multiply that cost dramatically.

The route label therefore used templates such as /orders/{order_id}, rather than the literal path of every individual order.

Customer IDs, order IDs, and operation IDs were kept out of metric labels. Those identifiers belonged in protected logs, traces, and business records.

Baodium used bounded labels for service-level dashboards and examined individual instances when the aggregate measurements showed a reason to investigate.

Modern Prometheus also supports native histograms, which can represent a histogram in one structured time series rather than separate classic bucket series.2

The chapter uses classic histograms because their bucket counters make the SLO calculations easy to examine.

Why the Median Was Misleading

During the incident, the median checkout latency in the affected region was approximately 0.8 seconds.

That looked reasonable.

The 99th percentile, however, had risen from about two seconds to 6.5 seconds.

The median told the engineers that half of requests completed within roughly 0.8 seconds.

The 99th percentile described the latency at or below which approximately 99 percent of requests completed.

The slowest one percent were experiencing much longer waits.

An average would have blended those requests with the fast majority, making the problem less obvious.

The engineers also needed a fleet-level measurement.

Averaging the 99th-percentile values reported by individual instances would not give a valid fleet percentile.

An instance handling one thousand requests and another handling fifty cannot contribute equally to the overall distribution.

A histogram allows the underlying bucket counts to be aggregated before the percentile is estimated.

Measuring Requests Within a Deadline

Baodium configured checkout duration buckets at

0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 100.1,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5,\ 100.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10

seconds, together with the implicit +Inf bucket.

The three-second bucket matched the checkout response objective.

That meant the team could calculate the fraction of completed request observations within three seconds from the bucket counter.

sum(
  rate(checkout_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
    le="3"
  }[5m])
)
/
sum(
  rate(checkout_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])
)

The function rate(...[5m]) estimates the per-second increase of a counter over the preceding five minutes.

The numerator counts observations whose duration fell within the configured three-second bucket.

The denominator counts all recorded request completions in the same eligible population, including requests that ended through failure or disconnection.

This query measures timeliness alone. The eventual SLI also needs to check whether the response represented an acceptable outcome.

The fleet-level 99th percentile uses a different calculation.

histogram_quantile(
  0.99,
  sum by (le, region) (
    rate(checkout_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
  )
)

The query aggregates bucket rates across instances before estimating each region’s percentile.

With a classic histogram, the estimate depends on the selected bucket boundaries.

The dashboard therefore displayed request counts alongside percentiles. A 99th percentile derived from forty requests is much less stable than one derived from hundreds of thousands.

There was still another measurement gap.

A histogram records a request when its observed interval ends. A request that has been waiting for several minutes has not yet contributed to the completed duration distribution.

Baodium also tracked requests currently in progress and the age of the oldest active request.

Those gauges helped engineers detect growing waits before the affected requests finally timed out.

Distributed Tracing and the Checkout Investigation

The metrics established that the slowest checkouts were taking considerably longer in one region.

The engineer next needed to understand what those requests were waiting for.

A distributed trace records operations performed during one execution.

Each recorded operation is called a span. It has a start time, an end time, an identity, and attributes describing the operation.

Spans also identify their relationships, allowing the tracing backend to assemble a request path through several services.

For checkout, the trace might contain a gateway span, an Order Service span, database operations, a Payment Service call, and several provider attempts.

The tracing backend could show these operations on a timeline.

An engineer might reach a representative slow trace from a histogram exemplar.

An exemplar associates a metric observation with contextual information such as a trace ID. It can help connect a latency measurement to one request that contributed to the distribution.

That trace must actually have been retained and indexed. Sampling or collection failures can leave an exemplar without a retrievable trace, so the interface must handle that case.

Connection Acquisition and Occupancy

The first trace the engineer opened showed a long database operation.

At first glance, that might suggest a slow SQL query.

The slow-query log, however, showed no corresponding increase in execution time.

The engineers had instrumented connection acquisition and connection occupancy separately, following the measurements introduced in Chapter 1.

The distinction appears in the following Python example.

The first span measures the time needed to acquire a connection.

If acquisition fails, the second span is never started.

The occupancy span begins once the connection has been acquired and ends after the code returns it to the pool.

Any SQL operations inside do_work can create their own child spans.

The example uses a synchronous connection pool. A production implementation would also record acquisition failures, timeouts, and any cleanup failures according to the database client’s actual behavior.

Reading the Slow Trace

Figure Figure shows an illustrative checkout trace that lasted approximately 5.2 seconds.

The request first spent 1.8 seconds waiting for a database connection.

After acquiring one, Order Service recorded its local acceptance state and called Payment Service while still occupying the connection.

The first payment attempt timed out after 1.5 seconds.

The retry policy waited 0.2 seconds, and the next attempt, using the same payment idempotency key, completed after 1.4 seconds.

The remaining processing and response handling accounted for approximately 0.3 seconds.

Those intervals sum to the illustrated 5.2-second path.

The important finding was the placement of the Payment Service call.

Order Service had acquired a database connection for its local transaction but had not released it before making the remote call.

While Payment Service waited for the provider, Order Service continued occupying a PostgreSQL connection.

When the provider became slower, those connections were occupied for longer.

Other checkouts then waited for a free connection before their own queries could begin.

This explained why the database acquisition metric increased even though individual SQL statements were still executing normally.

Chapter 3 had already corrected a similar issue in Payment Service, but Order Service still contained the same kind of dependency inside its database connection lifetime.

The trace showed where the time was spent. The pool metrics and provider latency measurements helped confirm the cause across many requests.

A single slow trace would not establish how often this pattern occurred or whether other database operations were contributing.

Overlapping Spans and the Critical Path

There is a common mistake when reading traces.

If a connection occupancy span contains a Payment Service span, adding their durations counts the payment interval twice.

The provider attempt spans may be children of the Payment Service span, adding another layer of overlap.

Parallel operations create a similar problem because two spans can run at the same time.

The critical path is the sequence of dependent operations that determines when the request can finish.

For this checkout, connection acquisition, provider attempts, and retry delay were all on that path.

Improving an operation outside the critical path might reduce resource usage without reducing the time needed to return the response.

The trace also needed careful interpretation when spans were missing.

A long gap between recorded operations might represent application code without instrumentation, thread scheduling, or another form of waiting.

A CPU profile, runtime metrics, or additional instrumentation could help distinguish those cases.

Clock differences between machines can also distort the apparent relationship between spans recorded on different hosts.

Traces give engineers a powerful timeline, but the timeline is only as complete and accurate as the recorded spans and clocks allow.

OpenTelemetry Instrumentation

Baodium needed consistent tracing across its services.

The platform team used OpenTelemetry so application teams could instrument operations without embedding a particular tracing backend into their business code.

OpenTelemetry separates the instrumentation API from the SDK that processes and exports telemetry.

An application library can use the API to describe an operation.

The application configures an SDK to record the resulting spans, apply sampling, and export them through the selected pipeline.

Instrumentation libraries create spans for common operations such as incoming HTTP requests, outgoing HTTP calls, and database statements.

They cannot automatically establish every business detail.

An HTTP span may show that Payment Service returned status 200, but that does not tell the investigator whether the payment was authorized, declined, or still unresolved.

The application therefore added bounded business attributes such as checkout.outcome and payment.attempt.

Where OpenTelemetry already defines an appropriate semantic convention, the team used that convention.

For example, http.response.status_code describes the HTTP status without requiring each service to invent a different attribute name.

Shared naming conventions made cross-service queries and dashboard templates more reliable.

Trace Context Across Services

For a trace to continue through several services, each outgoing call must communicate its trace identity and current parent span.

OpenTelemetry supports the W3C Trace Context standard, including the traceparent header.

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

The header contains a format version, trace identifier, parent span identifier, and trace flags.

In this example, the final 01 indicates that the sampled flag is set.

Client instrumentation injects the context into outgoing requests, while server instrumentation extracts it and creates spans under the corresponding trace relationship.

Supported HTTP and gRPC libraries can handle much of this automatically.

Custom clients and background threads require more attention.

For example, Python’s asyncio.to_thread propagates the current context, while a direct ThreadPoolExecutor submission does not automatically carry the same context in every case.

If the context is lost, an engineer may see one trace end at the thread handoff and another trace begin where processing continued.

Message processing introduces another choice.

A background reconciliation job may start minutes after the checkout request has finished.

Rather than representing that delayed execution as one continuously running synchronous request, Baodium started a new trace for the worker and linked it to the originating operation.

Span links can preserve the relationship between producer and consumer executions without requiring one long-lived parent span.

Trusting Incoming Trace Context

The public gateway also needed a policy for incoming trace headers.

A customer can send arbitrary HTTP headers, including traceparent and baggage.

The platform should not allow untrusted clients to choose internal telemetry attributes or control trace retention without limits.

Baodium’s public gateway created new internal trace context for untrusted requests.

Any client-provided context was handled under the gateway’s explicit trust policy rather than forwarded unchanged.

The same rule applied to baggage fields, which could otherwise carry unbounded or sensitive data into logs and traces.

Connecting Requests to Business Operations

The customer’s checkout involved more than one HTTP request.

The original submission had its own gateway request identifier and trace.

The refresh created another request and another trace.

A reconciliation worker might start a third execution several minutes later.

All of these could belong to one intended purchase.

Chapter 3 introduced the durable operation identity that made those executions recognizable as parts of the same business action.

Baodium used three identifiers for correlation.

A request ID identified one HTTP exchange.

A trace ID identified one instrumented execution and its related spans.

An operation ID identified the durable business operation across submissions, retries, status requests, and recovery.

The operation identity existed before the first payment submission. The browser retained the checkout submission key across refreshes, and the server bound that key to a validated, durable payment operation.

On a repeated submission, Order Service authenticated the caller and checked the operation’s stored parameters before retrieving the earlier result.

Possessing an operation ID did not authorize another customer to retrieve it.

Matching Browser and Gateway Reports

There was a smaller correlation problem at the HTTP boundary.

A browser refresh could produce several requests for the same business operation.

Matching browser reports to gateway records using only the operation ID would be ambiguous.

Timestamps were also insufficient, since browser and server clocks could differ.

The gateway therefore exposed its request ID to the browser through an approved response metadata mechanism, such as a Server-Timing entry or a permitted response header.

The display instrumentation included that request ID with its report.

Where a response was received, the engineer could associate the browser’s display event with the specific gateway exchange.

If the response was lost entirely, the browser might have no returned request ID to report.

The original submission key and the gateway’s ingress record still provided other correlation paths, although the display outcome could remain unknown.

The team monitored matched reports, gateway-only records, and browser-only reports rather than assuming every record had a partner.

Structured Logs

Logs connected those identities with the business events that occurred after the original request ended.

Baodium used structured JSON records with stable event names and bounded outcome values.

{
  "event.name": "payment.authorization_attempt_finished",
  "service.name": "payment-service",
  "trace_id": "example-trace",
  "operation_ref": "example-token",
  "attempt": 1,
  "retry_owner": "payment-service",
  "outcome": "timeout",
  "duration_ms": 1500
}

The attempt outcome describes what Payment Service observed.

A timeout means that the service stopped waiting within its configured deadline.

It does not establish that the provider rejected the authorization or never processed it.

That distinction was central to the original payment incident.

The stable event name also meant that the support tool could retrieve the same kind of record across application versions.

The logs provided the trace ID for the request execution and the protected operation reference for the longer business workflow.

Reconstructing the Customer’s Checkout

The support engineer could now search for the operation associated with the customer’s order.

The results included the original HTTP request, the refresh, payment attempts, durable state transitions, and the email delivery record.

Table Table shows the reconstructed timeline.

The timeline answered several questions that the original dashboard could not.

Request A disconnected after 4.5 seconds, but processing continued and the order was confirmed at 5.0 seconds.

That explained why the gateway reported a disconnected request while the database contained a confirmed purchase.

Request B did not create another order. Order Service recognized the same business operation and returned its pending status.

The available browser report confirmed that the pending page was displayed for request B. There was no corresponding display report for a confirmation from request A.

Together with the customer’s account, this explained the confusing interface experience, although the absence of a browser report alone could not prove exactly what the customer saw.

There was one remaining question. Had the provider authorized the payment more than once?

Baodium’s local records could not answer that conclusively because attempt 1 had timed out.

The engineer used the provider’s status-retrieval mechanism under the original idempotency key.

Under the provider contract used in this example, the key was recognized for 24 hours.

The provider reported one authorization, and its attempt records identified the later response as a replay of that result.

The customer had one authorized payment associated with the order.

The investigation could now distinguish a duplicate submission attempt from a duplicate financial effect.

The confirmation email had been published through the transactional outbox described in Chapter 3. The email consumer used its message identity to recognize possible redelivery.

That completed the support investigation.

The same evidence also gave the engineering team a more important finding: Order Service occupied database connections while waiting for Payment Service.

The customer had reported a missing confirmation. The investigation uncovered a resource-management problem affecting other checkouts.

Sensitive Data in Telemetry

The correlation records were useful because they could be searched across services.

They also needed careful protection.

Application logs may be retained for weeks and read by engineers, support tools, and automated investigation systems.

They should not contain raw payment credentials, card information, authentication tokens, or unnecessary personal information.

Baodium represented the raw operation ID in telemetry using a protected operation_ref.

The reference was produced with an HMAC using SHA-256 and a secret managed by the organization’s key-management system.

Unlike a plain hash, the keyed reference could not be reproduced without access to the HMAC key.

This was useful when identifiers were externally visible, predictable, or otherwise sensitive.

The reference was used for correlation, not authorization.

A support lookup still verified the employee’s permission to access the underlying order.

The platform limited which services could derive the reference. Other services could receive the already derived value through an approved internal field without receiving the HMAC secret.

Key rotation required a versioned reference scheme. The support tool could retain the ability to search records produced under older active keys for the permitted log-retention period.

The team also used typed logging structures that accepted approved fields rather than automatically recording entire HTTP bodies.

Collectors applied additional filters for known sensitive attributes and patterns, although those filters could not guarantee that every secret would be detected.

Access controls, retention limits, and staging tests provided further protection.

A recurring test injected synthetic sensitive values into staging requests and checked that those values were absent from the retained telemetry.

Sampling and Telemetry Cost

As Baodium added instrumentation, its observability bill increased.

The platform team needed to retain enough detail for investigations without collecting everything indefinitely.

Metrics, logs, and traces consumed resources in different ways, so each required a separate retention and volume policy.

Metric Retention and Aggregation

For metrics, cardinality was a major source of cost.

The team limited labels, removed unused measurements, and used recording rules for queries that dashboards executed repeatedly.

For example, the fleet-level checkout percentile could be calculated periodically and stored as a small derived series for dashboard use.

Prometheus and Thanos retained recent raw data at high resolution. Older measurements were available through lower-resolution downsampled data where the reporting requirements allowed it.

The release and incident dashboards continued using the resolution needed for their evaluation windows.

Log Volume and Retention

Logs had a different problem.

A health check executed every few seconds across hundreds of instances could generate millions of routine access records each day.

The team reduced unnecessary successful health-check logging and avoided verbose debug messages on every production request.

Warnings, errors, and important business events, including payment attempt outcomes, continued to be recorded under the required retention and sampling policies.

Baodium kept logs searchable for fourteen days.

Older records were archived to lower-cost object storage where the business and compliance requirements permitted it.

Archived logs were slower to query, which the incident response procedure had to account for.

Head and Tail Sampling

Traces presented another tradeoff.

At a peak of 500 checkout requests per second, with about twelve spans per request, the system could produce approximately

500×12=6,000500 \times 12 = 6{,}000500×12=6,000

spans per second.

At roughly one kilobyte per span, a full day at that constant peak would produce about 500 gigabytes of trace data before storage overhead and compression.

The actual daily average was closer to 200 requests per second, or roughly 200 gigabytes per day under the same assumptions.

Keeping every trace would be expensive.

With head sampling, the sampling decision is made near the start of a trace, before the final outcome is known.

That is relatively inexpensive, but the system may discard a request that later becomes important.

With tail sampling, the collector retains spans temporarily and makes the decision after observing more of the trace.

That can preserve slow or failed requests that head sampling might otherwise discard.

It also means the application must still create and export enough spans for the collector to make that decision.

The collector needs memory for pending traces, and the policy must handle traces that arrive late or remain incomplete.

Baodium used tail sampling for checkout.

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 3500
    spike_limit_mib: 700

  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 15s
    num_traces: 50000
    expected_new_traces_per_sec: 600
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code:
          status_codes: [ERROR]

      - name: slow
        type: latency
        latency:
          threshold_ms: 3000

      - name: pending-or-failed
        type: string_attribute
        string_attribute:
          key: checkout.outcome
          values: [pending, failed]

      - name: retried
        type: numeric_attribute
        numeric_attribute:
          key: payment.attempt
          min_value: 2
          max_value: 10

      - name: baseline
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic:
          sampling_percentage: 5

The policy attempted to retain traces containing errors, slow requests, pending or failed outcomes, and repeated payment attempts.

It also retained a small sample of ordinary requests for comparison.

The configuration is an excerpt from the collector processing policy. The complete deployment must also configure receivers, exporters, pipelines, and appropriate routing.

If roughly three percent of traces match the special-retention conditions, and the remaining traces are sampled at five percent, the resulting retention rate is approximately eight percent.

That would reduce about 200 gigabytes of daily raw trace volume to roughly 16 gigabytes, before considering compression and storage overhead.

The collectors also needed enough capacity for the temporary decision window.

At 600 new traces per second and a fifteen-second decision interval, one collector could have approximately 9,000 traces awaiting a decision under steady peak conditions.

The num_traces setting allowed additional space for bursts, while the memory limiter reduced the risk of unbounded collector memory consumption.

Sampling could still lose important evidence if the collector overloaded, crashed, or received only part of a trace.

Keeping the Spans of One Trace Together

Tail sampling requires the collector making the decision to receive the relevant spans for that trace.

If a gateway load balancer distributes individual spans arbitrarily, different collectors may each receive only part of the same execution.

Their decisions could then be incomplete or inconsistent.

Baodium routed trace traffic by trace ID through the collector load-balancing layer so spans belonging to the same trace reached the same decision processor under normal operation.

Routing changes, collector failures, and late arrivals still required monitoring.

The platform recorded dropped spans, exporter failures, and incomplete sampling decisions.

There was also an important interpretation rule.

Because the sampling policy retained many failed traces while retaining only some successful ones, the trace store could not be used to calculate the overall checkout failure rate.

That rate came from request metrics and durable operation records, whose collection contract covered the full eligible population.

SLIs, SLOs, and Customer Outcomes

The support ticket had been resolved, but the engineering team had another question.

How many customers had experienced the same uncertainty without contacting support?

The checkout dashboard needed a way to measure whether customers received the service Baodium had promised.

A service level indicator, or SLI, measures a specified aspect of service behavior.

A service level objective, or SLO, defines the target for that indicator over an evaluation period.

For a request-based indicator, we can express the result as

SLI=good eligible eventsall eligible events.\text{SLI} = \frac{\text{good eligible events}} {\text{all eligible events}}.SLI=all eligible eventsgood eligible events​.

The important engineering decisions are the definitions of good and eligible.

A service can report very high availability if it counts only requests that reached a healthy application instance.

That measurement would miss requests rejected before they reached the instance and requests lost during gateway failures.

Baodium defined indicators around the checkout journey rather than around individual component health.

Response, Status, and Resolution

The customer needed a timely response, a reliable way to retrieve the operation’s state, and an eventual final outcome.

Baodium defined three indicators.

Checkout response.

The fraction of eligible checkout submissions for which the gateway returned an acceptable response within three seconds.

An acceptable response was a confirmation, a definitive business rejection, or a durable pending result with a usable status reference.

Target: 99 percent over 30 days.

Operation status.

The fraction of authorized status requests that returned HTTP 200 with the operation’s state within one second.

The response could use a cached status subject to an independently tested maximum staleness of two seconds.

Target: 99.9 percent over 30 days.

Operation resolution.

The fraction of accepted checkout operations that reached a final outcome within fifteen minutes of acceptance.

Manual risk reviews followed their separately defined 24-hour workflow and evaluation population.

Target: 99.5 percent over 30 days.

A checkout could satisfy the response objective by returning a pending result quickly.

If the operation then remained unresolved for an hour, the resolution indicator would report that failure.

Likewise, an operation might complete successfully while its status endpoint remained unavailable.

The status indicator would detect that customer-facing problem even though the operation itself was confirmed.

Each indicator therefore covered a distinct part of the customer experience.

Business Rejections and Pending Responses

An HTTP error code does not always describe whether the service behaved correctly.

A payment provider may decline a card under its normal business rules.

If checkout returns a clear, timely rejection, the response can be considered good for the response SLI.

The purchase was unsuccessful, but the system provided the decision the customer needed.

A generic “try again” response is different when the previous payment outcome is uncertain.

That response can encourage a second authorization, as Chapter 3 showed.

A pending response also has conditions.

It can count as good only when the operation was durably accepted and the customer received a usable reference for checking its progress.

Returning 202 Accepted without recording the operation would create an apparent success with no durable work behind it.

The SLI definition therefore needs to agree with the API’s business contract.

Eligible Requests and Missing Results

For the checkout response indicator, Baodium counted authenticated, well-formed checkout submissions that reached its gateway.

Capacity rejections after that eligibility boundary, upstream errors, timeouts, and client disconnections were bad outcomes unless the documented contract provided an acceptable completed response.

Malformed and unauthenticated requests were excluded from this particular population.

Their volumes were monitored separately so that a sudden increase would still be visible.

The gateway recorded failures that individual application processes might miss.

However, a gateway could also crash before recording a request.

The platform therefore compared load-balancer request observations with gateway totals and used browser submission reports and external probes as additional evidence.

Those sources did not always provide exact one-to-one counts, so unexplained differences became coverage investigations rather than automatically classified successes.

Implementing the Indicators

The checkout response indicator used the gateway’s classic histogram.

Because the three-second bucket was explicitly configured, the team could count acceptable outcomes completed within the target.

sum(
  increase(checkout_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
    le="3",
    outcome=~"confirmed|rejected|pending"
  }[30d])
)
/
sum(
  increase(checkout_request_duration_seconds_count[30d])
)

The expression assumes the histogram covers the documented eligible request population and that outcomes are classified consistently at the gateway.

The numerator counts acceptable responses within three seconds.

The denominator includes all eligible observed requests, including failed and disconnected requests.

For operational efficiency, the team calculated hourly good and eligible totals with recording rules and aggregated them over the SLO window.

The underlying counts remained available for auditing.

Status Correctness

The status indicator used a similar one-second duration bucket for the status route.

Production requests were the source because a probe that always retrieved one healthy test order could miss failures affecting specific customer operations.

A timely HTTP 200 response still did not prove the returned state was correct.

Baodium therefore included a state version in status responses and sampled a small proportion of them for consistency checking.

The checker compared the returned version and state with the durable transition history.

It also checked whether a newer state had been committed more than the permitted two-second staleness interval before the response was served.

The timestamps came from systems with a documented clock-synchronization policy, and the verification procedure accounted for possible measurement uncertainty.

Comparing a previous response against the operation’s current state would not be sufficient.

The operation might have changed legitimately after the response was sent.

The checker needed to evaluate the state that was valid at the response’s observation time.

The sampled correctness result had its own alert and coverage measurement. It was reported separately from the full-population timeliness SLI.

Resolution From Durable Operations

The resolution indicator could not be calculated from the original HTTP request histogram.

A checkout might be accepted now and finish ten minutes later.

The gateway’s request duration would already have been recorded.

Baodium used a background evaluator that read durable operation records.

Every accepted operation had an acceptance time and a deadline for its required final outcome.

After the deadline passed, the evaluator checked the first durable transition into a terminal state.

If the operation had completed within the allowed interval, the evaluation was good.

If it completed late or remained unresolved, the evaluation was bad.

The evaluator wrote a durable result keyed by operation ID, preventing duplicate evaluations when several workers retried the same work.

Aggregate metrics were derived from those evaluation records.

That was safer than relying only on an in-memory counter incremented after an evaluation committed.

The system also reported the number and oldest age of operations awaiting evaluation.

Otherwise, a stalled evaluator could stop producing bad events at exactly the moment the resolution SLI needed them.

Finding Gaps in Monitoring Coverage

The indicators were useful only while their observations were available.

Baodium therefore monitored the measurement paths themselves.

This changed how the on-call team interpreted quiet dashboards.

An empty failure graph could mean that no failures occurred.

It could also mean that the application or monitoring pipeline had stopped reporting.

The team needed a separate signal for those situations, particularly on low-traffic services and during network outages.

Error Budgets and Alerting

Once the team had defined its indicators, it could decide when reliability had degraded enough to require action.

An SLO of 99.9 percent allows 0.1 percent of eligible events to be bad over the evaluation period.

That allowance is the error budget.

For one million eligible status requests over thirty days, the permitted number of bad results is

1,000,000×0.001=1,000.1{,}000{,}000 \times 0.001 = 1{,}000.1,000,000×0.001=1,000.

This includes the failures caused by releases, dependencies, and ordinary service operation.

The budget does not suggest that those failures are desirable. It provides a common measure for evaluating reliability and release risk.

The next question was how quickly the team was using that allowance.

Burn Rate

The burn rate compares the observed bad-event fraction with the fraction permitted by the SLO.

burn rate=observed bad-event fraction1−SLO target.\text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed bad-event fraction}} {1-\text{SLO target}}.burn rate=1−SLO targetobserved bad-event fraction​.

Suppose the status endpoint produced 1,300 bad results among one million requests.

The observed bad-event fraction would be 0.13 percent, against an allowed 0.1 percent.

The burn rate would therefore be 1.3.

If that rate continued, the equivalent thirty-day budget would be consumed in about 23 days.

The evaluation window matters. A five-minute burn rate describes a recent problem. A thirty-day value describes performance across the objective period.

Baodium used multiple windows to distinguish rapid outages from slower, persistent failures.

Fast-Burn Alerts

The platform team wanted to page when the status endpoint consumed roughly two percent of its thirty-day error budget in one hour.

Thirty days contain 720 hours.

Two percent of that budget used in one hour corresponds to a burn rate of

0.02×720=14.4.0.02 \times 720 = 14.4.0.02×720=14.4.

For the 99.9 percent status SLO, the corresponding bad-event fraction is

14.4×0.001=0.0144.14.4 \times 0.001 = 0.0144.14.4×0.001=0.0144.

That is 1.44 percent.

The team used a long one-hour window and a shorter five-minute window.

Both had to exceed the threshold before the fast-burn alert fired.

This prevented an old, recovered failure from continuing to page simply because it was still included in the preceding hour.

The following Prometheus rule excerpt assumes a one-second histogram bucket and an ok outcome for acceptable status responses.

- record: status:bad_ratio:rate5m
  expr: |
    1 -
    sum(rate(status_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
      le="1", outcome="ok"
    }[5m]))
    /
    sum(rate(status_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

- record: status:bad_ratio:rate1h
  expr: |
    1 -
    sum(rate(status_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
      le="1", outcome="ok"
    }[1h]))
    /
    sum(rate(status_request_duration_seconds_count[1h]))

- alert: StatusFastBurn
  expr: |
    (
      status:bad_ratio:rate1h > 14.4 * 0.001
      and
      status:bad_ratio:rate5m > 14.4 * 0.001
    )
    and
    sum(increase(
      status_request_duration_seconds_count[1h]
    )) >= 500
  labels:
    severity: page

The threshold came from the budget the team was willing to spend before paging.

The one-hour window measured substantial recent budget consumption, while the five-minute window checked whether the problem was still active.

The minimum request count reduced noisy ratios at very low traffic volumes.

The rule still needed testing against real incident and baseline traffic, including missing series and zero denominators.

Google’s SRE Workbook develops this multi-window burn-rate approach and provides additional paging and ticket thresholds.3

Slow-Burn Alerts

A service could consume its budget steadily without ever reaching the fast-burn threshold.

For example, a burn rate of two would consume a thirty-day budget in approximately fifteen days if sustained.

That deserved attention even though it was far below 14.4.

Baodium added a ticket-level alert for a burn rate above one over both three days and six hours.

The longer window identified persistent degradation, and the shorter one required the problem to continue.

The team also handled low-volume services separately.

If an endpoint received only twenty requests in an hour, one failure would produce a five-percent bad-event fraction.

That could generate a large apparent burn rate without enough evidence for the same paging policy used on busy checkout traffic.

The platform used minimum volume gates and separate absolute-failure or synthetic-probe rules for low-volume cases.

Missing measurements had their own alerts.

A burn-rate expression with no input series might return no result and never fire.

The team monitored metric availability, gateway traffic coverage, and unexpected absence of requests during periods that normally had traffic.

A page included the affected region, recent bad and eligible totals, deployment versions, and links to the dashboard and runbook.

Alertmanager grouped related component failures so an incident affecting many instances did not produce a separate page for every container.

Testing Whether Monitoring Actually Works

By this point, Baodium had added several measurements that would matter only when something failed.

That created a testing problem.

The provider timeout path might execute rarely under normal traffic. A client disconnect could occur between two ordinary instrumentation steps.

A recovery worker might stop after committing a record but before reporting its completion.

The team could not assume those cases were measured correctly simply because ordinary checkout tests passed.

It introduced failure-injection tests that checked the resulting telemetry as well as the application behavior.

Provider timeout.

A stub provider delayed an authorization response beyond the attempt deadline.

The payment log and span had to report a timeout without treating the provider result as a definitive decline.

Recovery had to retain the original operation identity.

Worker crash.

A worker was terminated after the acceptance record committed.

The operation had to remain discoverable, and the resolution evaluator had to classify it correctly after the deadline.

Client disconnect.

A test client closed its connection while checkout was still processing.

The gateway had to record the disconnected outcome, and the durable operation could continue under its own policy.

Pool exhaustion.

The test reduced the database pool to one connection and occupied it.

Another request had to show an acquisition wait before any SQL execution span began.

Unreadable status.

A controlled fault made one accepted operation’s status endpoint return an internal error.

The status indicator had to record the failed lookup even though other operations and the external test order continued working.

Each test included queries against the telemetry backend.

The test therefore verified that the expected evidence was recorded and could be found, subject to the sampling and collection contract.

One early pool-exhaustion test found a database client that recorded only SQL execution.

Its connection acquisition wait had been included in a generic database duration metric, making the earlier dashboard misleading.

The unreadable-status test exposed a different gap.

An external probe using one known order remained healthy while some customer operations could not be retrieved.

That confirmed why the status SLI had to include production request outcomes.

Field note

Facebook, October 2021

On October 4, 2021, Facebook experienced a major outage after a network-maintenance command unintentionally disconnected its global backbone.

An auditing system intended to prevent the unsafe command failed because of a software bug.

The loss of connectivity caused Facebook’s DNS infrastructure to withdraw its BGP advertisements, making its services unreachable from much of the internet.

The same incident affected internal tools and network access used by engineers investigating the failure. Recovery required personnel to reach the data centers physically before normal backbone connectivity could be restored.

The incident illustrates a problem that also applies to observability.

If monitoring, identity services, and recovery tools depend on the same network that has failed, the on-call team may lose access to the evidence and controls needed for recovery.

Baodium therefore needed independent external probes and a rehearsed recovery route for failures affecting the telemetry and identity infrastructure itself.

Source: Meta Engineering, October 5, 2021.

Measuring the Fix During a Canary

The checkout investigation showed that Order Service occupied a database connection while waiting for Payment Service.

The engineers changed the handler so its local transaction completed and its connection was returned before the remote call began.

That reduced the time each request needed a database connection.

The team tested the change under representative provider latency and request load, then introduced it through a canary deployment.

The canary measurements included connection-acquisition time, connection occupancy, checkout latency, pending outcomes, and unresolved-payment age.

A reduction in connection waits was useful evidence, but the release also needed to preserve payment correctness.

If the new implementation returned faster while increasing uncertain payments, the customer outcome had not improved.

The team therefore compared the resource measurements with the response, status, and resolution indicators before expanding exposure.

Design Exercise: Observability for Document Processing

Consider a document-processing API that accepts a file, extracts its text, adds the result to a search index, and notifies the customer when processing is complete.

The HTTP request may finish in less than a second, while the processing job takes several minutes.

How would we measure whether the service is operating correctly?

We can begin with the same observation boundaries used for checkout.

At the gateway, the API records whether the upload request was accepted and whether the client received a response.

The workflow store records the durable job identity and its state transitions.

The output side records whether the processed document can actually be retrieved or found through the promised search interface.

Those observations prove different things.

A successful upload response means the service accepted responsibility for the job under its API contract.

A worker completion record shows that a processing attempt finished its recorded step.

The customer needs the processed document to be available under the retrieval contract.

Suppose the worker uploads the extracted content to object storage, then crashes before committing the search-index update.

The object exists, but the customer cannot find the document.

A dashboard showing successful object uploads could suggest that processing was healthy.

The durable workflow record would reveal that the operation had not reached the customer-visible completion state.

Defining the Processing Indicator

One useful processing SLI is the fraction of accepted jobs that become retrievable within five minutes.

The denominator contains every accepted job whose five-minute evaluation deadline has passed.

That includes jobs that never started and jobs whose workers crashed.

The numerator contains those jobs for which the required output was durably committed and retrievable within the deadline.

A successful worker exit alone does not satisfy that requirement.

The API can also have an admission SLI measuring whether eligible upload requests receive a timely accepted response.

A separate correctness or recovery indicator may track operations that reach an incorrect terminal state or require manual repair.

These indicators can fail independently.

An API may accept uploads quickly while processing jobs fall behind. Workers may finish processing while the search index is unavailable.

The measurements need to distinguish those cases.

Tracing Deferred Work

The upload request and the later worker execution are separate processing intervals.

A stable job ID links them across requests, queue messages, and recovery attempts.

The application uses new traces or linked spans for deferred executions, while protected logs and durable workflow records retain the job identity.

The job ID does not belong in a Prometheus metric label.

Instead, the team aggregates metrics by bounded dimensions such as operation type, outcome, and error category.

When an engineer needs to inspect one unfinished document, the operation store provides the precise identity and state history.

A recovery worker can then determine which stages completed and which remain unresolved.

Summary

The customer who contacted Baodium support wanted to know whether a payment had gone through.

The original infrastructure dashboard could show that CPU was healthy and the provider had become slower. It could not establish what the customer had submitted, what the provider accepted, or which result the browser displayed.

The revised instrumentation connected the gateway requests, database transitions, payment attempts, browser reports, and recovery records through the same durable operation identity.

Metrics showed how widespread the problem was. Traces explained where the affected requests spent their time. Logs and authoritative records established what happened after the original request stopped waiting.

The team also needed to know when its own measurements were missing. A quiet dashboard could not be accepted as evidence of healthy service without monitoring coverage.

Once the engineers identified the resource waits and customer outcomes, they could evaluate the next design change with better evidence.

Chapter 9 takes those observations into admission control, rate limits, bulkheads, and the policies used to keep one overloaded dependency from consuming capacity needed by other operations.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The monitoring system provides sufficient evidence to evaluate checkout’s customer-facing commitments across request execution, durable state changes, and deferred recovery.
Condition that tests it & A request disconnects, an operation continues after its HTTP response ends, a status lookup returns an incorrect result, or part of the telemetry pipeline becomes unavailable.
Constraint or invariant & Committed state, gateway response, and browser display are separate observation boundaries.

Each indicator defines its eligible population, point of measurement, required good outcome, and treatment of missing evidence.

Telemetry sampling must not be used to infer full-population business success rates.
Evidence and uncertainty & Gateway records, database transitions, and provider reconciliation established the outcome of the investigated checkout.
Signal and evaluation window & Measure response, status, and resolution SLIs over their defined objective windows.

Evaluate fast and slow error-budget burn, request volume, monitoring coverage, unresolved-operation age, collector drops, and external-probe results during incidents and release tests.
Control and decision & Page on significant customer-facing budget consumption, open tickets for persistent low-rate degradation, and investigate missing telemetry separately.
Owner and review trigger & The checkout team defines business outcomes, durable operation evidence, and customer-facing SLIs.
